approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake and the west-side boot path
approach_variants.notes: The whole peak is a backpack with a short walk-up bolted onto the end of it. Nearly every party camps at or near Upper Cathedral Lake, around 7,380 ft, and climbs from there. The lake is reached most directly from the Andrews Creek Trailhead at the end of Forest Road 51, going in over Andrews Pass and along the Boundary Trail; the Chewuch River option out of Thirtymile is considerably longer and joins the same ground near Cathedral Pass. Once at the lake nothing about the climb is committing: it is grass, scree and boulder from the trail to the top, with the occasional short step where hands come out. Most parties tag Cathedral Peak the same day, and the two are linked by a connecting gully rather than a return to the lake between them.
approach_variants.season: Early July to late September
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes and summit plateau
Snow lingering in the access gullies and the upper basin into July
High, cold creek crossings on the approach during runoff
Open, treeless plateau with no shelter from afternoon storms
A long day's walk or more from the nearest road in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding: From Upper Cathedral Lake the trail runs southeast and rounds the low toe of Amphitheater's west ridge. Roughly half a mile along, at about 7,200 ft, a beaten boot path breaks off uphill and climbs grass and scree to the northeast. That boot path is the start of the climb, and it is the only prepared thing you will see between the lake and the top. If the trail is still contouring level, you have not reached it; if the trail begins to lose elevation steadily and the ridge above you falls back behind your shoulder, you have walked past it. The path leads into an open bowl at about 8,000 ft rimmed with broken rock, the amphitheater the mountain is named for, and once you are standing in that bowl you are on the route. Two things fool parties here. In early season a steep snow gully rises straight out of the lake basin toward the ridge crest, and it does work, but it is a harder and icier start than the boot path and it is not the standard line. And the summit mass is shaped like a T with several plateau rises on it, so the first high point you reach after leaving the bowl is often not the highest. Keep walking the plateau until the ground stops rising. The check on the other side is the rock: the dramatic spires standing north of the lake belong to Cathedral Peak, and if you are climbing toward them you are on the wrong mountain.

approach_variants.name: Azurite Pass, the 7,400 ft shoulder and the west-face traverse
approach_variants.notes: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse crosses a series of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, well marked with ducks and cairns, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock on the traverse and in the final gully — stay off each other's fall line
The final gully often holds snow into midsummer; ice axe, and crampons if icy
Two or three short snow runnels to cross on the west-face traverse
Many ribs and gullies that all look like viable options when seen obliquely from a distance
approach_variants.baseFinding: Turn up too late and you meet the southwest face — that is the error to watch for. The correct gully is narrow at its base and cannot be seen from the ridge, so parties keep traversing hoping for something obvious, run out onto the imposing southwest face, and find it goes Class 4 in a hurry. The stated fix from those who have made that mistake is to retreat to the last gully to the south and go up that. The right line stays loose and never harder than short steps of Class 3 for roughly the last 200 ft to the top: if you are climbing more than short sections of Class 4, you are off route, and if you have drifted onto cleaner, more solid rock high on the gully's climber's-left wall you have left the gully floor for steeper and more exposed ground. One gully on this line pinches to about three feet, tight enough to touch both walls with your arms out — that constriction is a confirmation you are in a real line, not a warning.

approach_variants.name: Shellrock Basin camp and the traverse to the east-face col
approach_variants.notes: Blackcap is a leg of a multi-day traverse rather than an objective on its own, and the walk in is measured in days, not hours. The usual staging is a camp in Shellrock Basin just below and east of Shellrock Pass, reached over Rolo Pass from Fred's Lake after a long valley approach up the Middle Fork Pasayten. From camp the peak is a half-day round trip on easy ground. Water is at the basin and in upper Eureka Creek and there is none on the mountain. An eastern line exists off the Monument Creek trail into the open Monument-Blackcap basin, but the Shellrock side is the travelled one and the one with a recognisable start.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the east face, worse descending than ascending
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
A steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass that can persist into early summer
High, cold fords of Eureka Creek and the Middle Fork Pasayten during runoff
Days from the nearest road with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a col, and getting to it is the only route-finding on the day. Leave the trail at Shellrock Pass itself and traverse south-southwest across the open grassy and rocky basin, keeping below the cliff bands the whole way. That traverse ends at the foot of a talus slope. Work the left, eastern edge of that talus southward until the cliff band above you finally runs out; the saddle at the end of it, directly beneath Blackcap's east face, is where the climbing starts. The confirmation is the rock itself and it is the clearest single marker on this peak: Blackcap's summit cap is near-black hornfels and shale sitting abruptly on top of much paler rock, and the colour boundary is visible from the col and is under your hands within a few minutes of leaving it. If everything around you is still light-coloured after several hundred feet of scree, you are on the wrong flank. Two ways to know you have overshot. Following the trail over Shellrock Pass and down its far side takes you away from the peak altogether. Continuing south past the end of the cliff band instead of turning up drops you toward the Monument basin. In early season a steep snowfield sits below the pass on this traverse and is normally bypassed on its left; carry an axe if it is still there.

approach_variants.name: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
approach_variants.notes:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend left up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse right through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
approach_variants.season: Climbed historically in early-to-mid August; the window is narrow because it depends on a stable, well-bridged icefall and on residual snow and ice in the summit gully
hazards: An icefall traversed on the approach, with crevasse and serac fall the standing hazard and the crossing itself described as frightening
A crumbly red rock stratum crossing the whole face at mid-height, which is where the rockfall comes from
Extreme remoteness — an incident on a 3,000 ft face this rarely climbed would be very hard to get help for
Heavy packs on class 4-5 ground, which the first-ascent account flags as compounding the difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding: The sequence is countable from bottom to top and it is the best thing this route has: easier cliffs, then a small glacier, then left up it to an icefall, then right through the icefall to the rock. The direction reverses — left to reach the icefall, right to get through it — and that reversal is what tells you the crossing you are making is the intended one. The rope-up point is a ledge system near the second prominent tree, where the ledge makes its first descent. An oddly specific marker, and a genuinely countable one if the trees are visible. The mid-route confirmation is a colour and it crosses the whole face: a prominent, crumbly red stratum at roughly half height. You cannot go round it — it spans the face — so meeting a red band of bad rock at mid-height is proof you are on the line and not beside it. It is also the crux and the rockfall source, so it is worth expecting. Between those two, follow the prominent central rib essentially straight up. Near the top a 100-ft notch is passed on steep snow or ice through a narrow gully angling across the rib, and then it is easier ground to the summit. And the negative test is the whole peak: Booker's other two routes are walks. If the ground you are on is class 2-3 talus, you are on the Northwest Route or the South Ridge — this is the only technical line on the mountain, and the first ascent said so in as many words.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Colonial Creek Campground (Thunder Creek Trailhead)

approach_variants.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. Fill up with water there — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
hazards: No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on an exposed ridge
Steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle, very sketchy when wet
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height
Hard snowfields at High Pass wanting crampons
Loose rubbly schist on the summit crest, with a fatal fall on record on this peak
Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail — hot, and blowdown
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical instruction on the traverse is about height, and it comes with a stated consequence: from the saddle south of Berge, curving right around the bowl toward the mountain, stay high. Drop too low and you end up in steep waterfall slabs. If you are looking at running water over slabby ground, you have lost too much elevation and should climb back.

The arrival is unmistakable and it is not rock: you reach a beautiful forested bench with larches — good enough that parties note it as a campsite — and cross a river. Once across that river you are at the base of Buck.

Above there the ground is broad pumice, talus and low-angle snowfield up to the south ridge around 7,400 ft, and then rubbly slabby schist along the crest with a short step up to Class 3-4 near a horn close to the top.

Summit warning, and it is a genuine unresolved disagreement rather than a caution: parties do not agree how many summits Buck has or which is highest. One party climbed the middle of the long crest, found the register there, and judged it higher than both the north point and the south by twenty feet or more. Another says the south is the true one. A third found the register — dated 1967 — on the north horn and reported the two tops as roughly equal. Only one of those parties actually measured anything. The summit crest holds several bumps within a few feet of each other, so expect to walk the crest rather than to arrive at an obvious high point, and do not treat a register as proof.

A useful sighting cue from a party approaching by a different line: the summit does not come into view until you reach the flat ground around 8,000 ft, in an upper cirque one climber described as looking like the flying bridge of a boat.

This mountain has killed someone — a climber fell fifty feet scrambling on a route on the east side, direct from Trinity, in 2018. The direct east line involves a river ford and a savage brushy bushwhack and is generally recommended as a descent rather than an ascent.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Several unmarked routes on one fourteen-hundred-foot wall; position under the summit is the only identifier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall; the first pitch exists mainly to escape the fall line
Dirt and moss-filled cracks through the middle section and teetering blocks near the top
Multi-day approach with no cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides with one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face
Retreat from anywhere on this trip is measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

From that view, drop a plumb line from the summit. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the rockfall line rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

Negative marker: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: At least four unmarked lines on one wall, two of them starting close together on the same buttress
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the climbing
Roughly half the pitches are at the upper end of the grade, with the crux on a corner low down
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger, not by reversing the climb
Multi-day approach and a retreat measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Several unmarked routes on one face, two of them on the same buttress
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger rather than the way you came up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
approach_variants.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large tailings pile around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its west side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
hazards: Several notches in the spur ridge, most of them Class 5 from below — picking the wrong one is the route's real crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier remnant, worst late summer
A short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge with no fixed protection
Standing dead timber and loose footing in the burn above the tailings pile
Two creek crossings that both run high in early-season melt, one of them dependent on a footbridge that may be out
approach_variants.baseFinding: The arrival test is a notch, and it is the best negative marker on this peak: several notches cut the spur ridge and most of them are class 5 from below. The one you want is the highest notch you can reach easily, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's right — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right. How you know you are under it: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer. The stream is the handrail from camp: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the outlet stream that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything. What happens immediately after the notch, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn left and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one. The last obstacle is one move, not a pitch. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled. A note on the route's name: the south-east in this route's aspect is the glacier remnant itself, which faces south-east from under the spur ridge on the peak's east side; the finish is on the upper north-east ridge. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
hazards: A mandatory, somewhat exposed hand-pulled cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River; the river is not reliably fordable
Blowdown on the Chilliwack River Trail, measured at roughly two hours per 1.5 miles in bad years
Crevasses and open moats on the Whatcom, Challenger and Crooked Thumb Glaciers
Loose class 4-5 rock throughout the upper route, described in trip reports as horribly loose
Weathered fixed tat on the north-ridge horn that should not be trusted without backing up
A 40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at the foot of a snow couloir on the northwest side, and the couloir is the only thing on the peak you can identify in cloud. From the moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, the line goes up a 40-45 degree northwest-facing snow couloir to the saddle just north of the peak. In fog, do not navigate by the summit; navigate by the fact that you are in a confined snow gully with rock walls on both sides, steepening steadily to about 45 degrees. If the ground opens out and flattens, you are on the glacier, not in the couloir.

Arrival at camp, which is the harder find: the camp is a lateral moraine, i.e. a ridge of rubble sitting on the ice, reached by descending through West Challenger Notch off the Challenger Glacier bench at about 8,100 ft. The notch is the crux of the navigation, not the couloir. You are through it when the ground stops dropping and you are standing on loose rock with ice on both sides.

Confirm on the climb: above the couloir the route works along loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles, and the crux is a single roughly 10 ft near-vertical crack, 5.8+ or 5.2 with a point of aid, taken at the top of a headwall. A rock horn draped with old slings sits below those pinnacles. If you have climbed the couloir and are on clean, moderate rock with good stances, you are not on this route; everything here is described as horribly loose.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Challenger Glacier past the 8,100 ft bench instead of dropping through the notch takes you toward Challenger's own summit rocks, which is a different peak.

approach_variants.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.
approach_variants.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
hazards: The Bean Creek ford runs cold and pushy in May and June and is the real decision point of the day
Old avalanche debris crosses the trail just above the ford
Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge, easy to kick down onto a party below
No dependable water above the meadows
Steep, icy south-facing snow on a spring ascent
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the saddle, straight on goes somewhere else and the peak is left and straight up. Above the flower basin the tread goes intermittent through upper meadows and switchbacks to a broad, largely treeless saddle on the divide between the two drainages, around 6,200 ft, with scattered flat tent sites on it. The climbers' track up the peak is obvious underfoot but carries no marker of any kind — no cairn, no post, no blazed tree — so the test is the fork rather than a landmark: carrying straight on to the east takes you toward the far creek and away from the mountain, while the summit line turns left, to the north, and goes straight up the ridge. If you are still among flower meadow and old-growth stands you are in the basin below and have not reached the saddle at all. The upper ridge is roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting loose scree, sand and broken rock with the track fading in and out. Accounts disagree about whether there is one false top or several undulating bumps below the summit, so treat any high point with more ridge rising beyond it as another bump rather than the end.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a boot path dug into it in places — kicked rock runs straight onto anyone below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies present themselves and the correct one is hidden until you round a buttress
The whole summit area is small and becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
The south point is a steeply inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the East Face
Sub-summits nearby are convincing enough that parties have tagged them by mistake
No water once you leave the meadow
approach_variants.baseFinding: The small boggy meadow where the trail turns sharply left is the departure. From the meadow camp, follow the tread north until it turns sharply left at a small boggy meadow around 6,900 ft — past that turn the trail carries on around the south shoulder of the neighbouring peak, which is not where you are going. Leave it there and climb north, or slightly east of due north, over open ground almost to the ridge crest between the two peaks. Just before the crest, look for a scree and talus slope leading up and to the right to a notch on the northwest ridge. Take that about halfway, then cut right and south into the adjacent gully, and climb it to the depression between the two summits. Expect to see several gullies on the way in and not the one you want: it stays hidden until you round a buttress, and cairns only start marking the way once you are past that corner. The true summit is the north point, to the left of the depression as you arrive. Do not use a register to settle which point you are on — parties have found none on either.

approach_variants.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
approach_variants.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
hazards: No water at all beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
A scree gully to descend off the col, and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
The ridge is long, open and fully exposed to afternoon weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: A larch forest and then Fifth of July Pass is the gateway to the south ridge. After the boulder basin and the small larch meadow put you back on the ridge, the ground drops gradually and you walk through a larch forest immediately before arriving at Fifth of July Pass — that named saddle is where the south ridge begins, and the larch immediately below it is the confirmation. From the pass the south ridge is straightforward, with tree debris to avoid, and a short traverse along a long, broken ridgetop reaches the high point. The negative marker is the neighbouring tower: Devils Smoke Stack is a separate and harder summit with a sheer north side, climbed by steep gullies on its south with two tall steps of choss, and it lies on the far side of the intervening peak. You cannot arrive at one thinking it is the other without crossing that peak in between — so if the ground ahead rears into a tower with sheer cliffs on its north and no walkable line, you are back at the Smoke Stack rather than on this mountain's long broken crest.

approach_variants.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
approach_variants.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Off-trail navigation with no tread and no user path through the woods
Two distinct ways to end up in the wrong basin, both described below
A 600 ft descent off the divide into the creek that must be reclimbed on the return
Talus that starts as large solid boulders and degrades into fist- to football-sized rock that moves underfoot
The rock throughout is loose rubbly gneiss on lower-angle slopes
The north side of the true summit is craggy enough to block a traverse to the lower north point
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two elevations tell you you are in the wrong place, and both are worth memorising. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp
approach_variants.notes:
White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft — subject to the same long-running road access problems as the Sitkum approach, so confirm before relying on it. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT about three miles — roughly two thirds of a mile past the Kennedy Creek crossing, which is your water — to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: long-running road access problems on the White Chuck side
unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. That saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are not visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

approach_variants.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
very long PCT approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the Kennedy Ridge variation
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
approach_variants.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: twenty-mile-plus approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the other variations
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
approach_variants.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
hazards: An upper glacier described by parties as a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses that needs deliberate, slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left beneath the Kennedy Peak wall, where some parties have had to belay off bare glacier ice
Trading crevasse navigation for rockfall by hugging the left wall — the simplification is real and so is the cost
A bergschrund at the head of the glacier whose only crossing may be a single bridge found from the snow dome above it
8,200 ft of gain from a trailhead served by a road that has been closed at milepost 3.7, so the walk in may be far longer than the mileage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climb is below you, not above you, and that is the whole test. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go down off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

Arrival: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep right; on the upper glacier take the centre. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

The discriminator against Frostbite Ridge, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the ridge. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

The top end, and it is a real decision point: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing left to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay left of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

What hugging the left wall costs: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
approach_variants.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite with a documented fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The cliffs are the marker, and the instruction is to overshoot them by 100 ft. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further left past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

What confirms it once you are in: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the first chockstone, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A second chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

The exit test for later: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn left before the gully ends — look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

And one descent warning that parties get wrong: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the middle summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

approach_variants.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall is very likely and the peak has a documented history of fatalities from rockfall and breaking holds
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully — helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant rather than technical
Access: private property on the walking approach, closed to climbers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The gully is the obvious one on the south side, and the test is that it forces you out left. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

The confirmation is the chockstone, and it comes early. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' left out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

What the rock should feel like: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

And the negative test against its neighbours: the big west face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.

approach_variants.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.
approach_variants.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
hazards: a boundary crossing that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services
no water south of the creeks below the ridge junction
an exposed ridge camp
a 545 ft descent from camp that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
loose rock on the buttress
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From camp the route starts by losing height - about 545 ft down to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque. Any line that climbs from the camp is the wrong way. The saddle is the low point at the head of a bowl, with the cirque falling away in front of you and the buttress rising on its far side.

Recognise the cirque by its shape: it is an enclosed bowl beneath the north side of the peak, not an open flank. If the ground ahead of you drops away into a valley rather than into a bowl with walls around it, you have gone off the ridge too early or too late.

The buttress is on the north-east side, so from the saddle it should stand between you and the sun in the middle of the day rather than in it. A wall you approach in full afternoon sun is on the wrong aspect.

Check the peak: this is the north summit, the higher and broader of the two. The other main summit should lie to the south, connected by a rotten ridge that is not a usable link between them.

Water is the other fixed point. The last of it is the creeks in the forest below the ridge junction, well before camp. If you have passed those without filling, the correct move is to go back for water rather than to press on to a dry camp above a dry cirque.

approach_variants.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
hazards: an overgrown boundary swath that is steep, brushy and slow
a swamp low on the line
three thousand feet of unrelenting bushwhacking with no tread
no water on the upper half
reaching the ranger station depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The swath is the handrail - it is a cleared line through forest that runs east, and if you are not on it you are not on the approach. It is overgrown, so it looks like brush rather than like a corridor from inside it; the tell is that it is straight, and it does not wander with the terrain the way a game trail does.

A swamp is passed low down. Reaching it confirms the line; never reaching it means you have drifted off the swath into ordinary forest.

The join is a col near 6,300 ft, roughly three thousand feet above the start, where the swath's climbing ends against the ridge. From there the route is the same as the long approach: work along to the saddle at the head of the north cirque near 5,800 ft, which means losing height again, and the buttress stands on the far side of the bowl.

If you arrive on a ridge and the ground beyond is an open valley rather than an enclosed bowl, you are at the wrong col. The cirque is walled; the valley is not.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft either by walking seven or eight flat miles of the East Bank Trail from SR 20 or, far more often, by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of that. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to mid-September
hazards: Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe
Loose, fractured chert throughout, with little that will hold protection
Steep forest with cliff bands on the approach, far worse to descend than to climb
Wet slabs and a pitch of low fifth class where the glacier meets the ridge
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and on the snow traverse below the summit tower
Crevasses low on the glacier, and a moat where snow meets rock late in the season
Very remote, several days from a road in any direction, with no realistic quick rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding: Nobody climbs this ridge from its toe; you meet it partway up off the Nohokomeen Glacier, and exactly where to leave the ice is unsettled, so treat the aiming points below as the frame and read the ground. Climb the glacier up its centre, passing just to the right of the large rock that stands out on the ice, and head for the crest to the left of the summit tower rather than for the tower itself. The glacier runs out against rock at about 8,000 ft. The one unmistakable feature on the route is there: a hole clean through the rock, a keyhole big enough to squirm through, and that hole is how the crest is gained. Parties travelling in both directions have used it as their marker. Taken from the very top of the glacier the exit costs a pitch of wet, junky low fifth class and a scramble over greasy slabs, and the party who did it that way came away convinced an easier line onto the crest exists a little lower down, short of the glacier's top edge, so it is worth traversing under the rock and looking rather than forcing the highest weakness. Above the keyhole the confirmation is instant and unlike anything below it: a knife-edged crest of genuinely solid rock, which is rare on this mountain. If what is under your hands is fractured and rotten, you are not on the crest yet. One decoy matters. The north side's other line, the headwall, rises off the same glacier and tops out within minutes of the summit, so if the snow you are on runs straight to the top with no ridge left to travel, you are on the headwall and not this route. The North Ridge leaves the ice well below the summit and still has a long way to go: knife edge, then an exposed snow traverse south across and below the summit tower with occasional protection along the upper moat, and a final pitch of low fifth class up the East Ridge to the top at 9,066 ft.

approach_logistics.trailhead: May Creek (via Ross Lake shuttle) or East Bank Trail (alternative)

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt — the first is an ordinary ford at normal flow and a stopper at high water
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last several off any maintained trail, so a navigation error is measured in hours
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier that are unreadable under early-season cover
Road closures on FR-49 and the Mountain Loop Highway that can shut the west approach entirely, turning this into a much longer trip from the east
approach_variants.baseFinding: This route has two arrivals and they are different kinds of thing. The first is where glacier travel starts, and the second is where the scrambling starts. Confusing them is how a party ends up unroped in the wrong place. Glacier starts at foam pass. From camp climb to Foam Pass and step onto the White Chuck Glacier. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure. Scrambling starts at the 7,400 ft saddle, and you get there by counting rather than by looking. Off the glacier, gain the flat shoulder near 6,000 ft; follow the connecting ridge north-north-west over a bulge at 7,200 ft; cross the small basin below the east summit; then go west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. Shoulder, bulge, basin, saddle — four things in that order. If you have gone west without first crossing a basin, you are on the wrong side of the bulge. The arrival test at the saddle: from it, one ridge runs away from you forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque. That ridge is the route. If the ground ahead does not have a glacier cirque falling away on one side of it, you are not on the saddle you want. What too far looks like: continuing east instead of west from the 7,200 ft bulge takes you to the east summit rather than the summit ridge — and of the twin tops on the summit ridge the eastern one is the true high point by only 10-15 ft, so bag both. One thing to expect on the ice rather than look for: a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice, a shallow icefall, on the White River Glacier. It is a crampon problem, not a navigation one, but it is the reason the descent takes longer than the map suggests.

approach_variants.name: Lake of the Woods camp and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail on the mountain itself; the whole climb is talus, scree and boulder-field walking off a high camp. The usual staging is a camp around 6,600 ft near Lake of the Woods, reached over Pistol Pass on the long-abandoned Pistol Ridge tread out of the Monument Creek valley. That approach has been unmaintained for decades and involves an unbridged ford of Eureka Creek that runs thigh to waist deep during snowmelt. A longer alternative from the Slate Pass road end reaches the same country by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and avoids that ford, at the cost of tread that is harder still to follow. From camp the peak is a couple of hours each way for a fit party, and most parties pair it with Monument Peak.
approach_variants.season: July to early October
hazards: Loose talus near the summit
Short exposed sections of blocky granite on the ridge
Unbridged ford of Eureka Creek, dangerous during snowmelt
Abandoned, brushy, deadfall-choked approach tread navigated by cairns
Steep north wall and northeast face immediately off the standard line
No cell service and multi-day self-rescue distance
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp near Lake of the Woods, head uphill out of the lake basin toward the peak, which rises directly above camp. The base is where the open slope steepens toward the summit, and the mountain tells you where that is by refusing the obvious line. A subsidiary rock knob blocks a direct ascent from the south, and a cliff band bars a straight finish near 8,000 ft, so if you are looking up at a clean unbroken slope from the south side you are not below the standard start and pushing on will cliff you out. Bend instead onto the mountain's lower east ridge. That ridge is identifiable at its foot by larch: the lower slopes are studded with scattered larch groves, and the climbing proper begins where the larches thin out around 7,800 ft and the ground turns to boulder-hopping and coarse scree. Several gullies of much the same difficulty run up from there and any of them will go; take the one where hands come out only occasionally and the footing stays blocky rather than sliding. Early sections often feel like a staircase of granite blocks, which is a good sign you are on the ridge rather than in a scree runnel beside it. Two warnings on where not to be. The north wall and the northeast face are appreciably steeper and are not part of this route, so if the ground ahead drops away rather than rising, move back south. And the last few hundred feet hold snow late; footprints in it are a reasonable line but not proof of a good one.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
approach_variants.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
approach_variants.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts directly above the gap. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an open bench, and above the bench you cross a snowfield into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's left for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
approach_variants.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Remote with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, work into the peak's northeast basin. The route is guarded by a ridge notch, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a large vertical crack forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. If the notch you have reached can be walked through, it is not this one. Above the notch the ground eases and joins the snowfield and cirque used by the trail approach. Negative marker: if you are standing in a broad trail saddle with tread underfoot, you are at Dutch Miller Gap and on the standard line, where no such crack step exists.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
approach_variants.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford below the lake: cold and swift, and serious in snowmelt
Chief Creek ford near the head of Waptus Lake
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Very long approach far from help, with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming up from Lake Ivanhoe you climb to the gap from the east, so the check is that the trail has stopped climbing and starts to drop west toward the Middle Fork, with the peak above you on the left. The climbing starts at the first heather and rock steps above the gap and leads to an open bench, then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face.
