Negative marker: if you are still beside Lake Ivanhoe or below it, you have not reached the gap yet.

approach_variants.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
approach_variants.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
the Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
loose blocks on the summit ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the reference, and it is the only place on this mountain where you can see both basins at once. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

approach_variants.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed until January 2028)
approach_variants.notes: Not usable while the Suiattle River Road stays closed at milepost 4 under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner; washouts cut off the Downey Creek Trailhead, and the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) also closes the trailhead and the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails from August 15 through December 31, 2026. Before the closure this was the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
hazards: road and trailhead cut off by washouts until at least January 2028
sustained blowdown and slide-alder bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
the Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
crevasse hazard on the Dana Glacier below Spire Col
multi-day evacuation distance with no cell coverage
loose blocks near the summit crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the reference, and it is the only place on this mountain where you can see both basins at once. Climbing out of the White Rock Lakes basin you reach a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Stay near the crest, and keep the party abreast rather than strung out directly below one another.

approach_variants.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
hazards: wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun - axe, crampons if firm, early season
heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
no reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
the ridge is unsafe wet and unsafe without rock gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge at the low notch on the West Ridge, near 5,800 ft, and that notch is where the technical climbing starts — nothing below it needs a rope.

Coming up from the basin, aim for a depression in the face beneath the notch. Climb easy class 3 ground up to that depression, then the slabby depression itself is the crux of the entry, class 4 to low fifth, and you bear right at the top of it to arrive in the notch. If you are climbing slab and it does not lead to a col within a rope length or two, you picked the wrong depression.

Negative markers. If you gained the crest somewhere that walks easily on both sides, you are on the ridge but past the notch and the climbing above will not match any description. And if you find yourself scrambling straight at the summit block instead of setting out along a ridge, you came up the south face rather than to the west ridge notch.

The ridge involves class 4 to mid fifth moves and wants rock gear. Do not attempt it wet.

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
hazards: exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
slide alder low down
no reliable water past the trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive directly at the low notch on the West Ridge, around 5,800 ft, which is where the technical climbing begins. Arriving by this line you should be traversing beneath the crest on the north (Commonwealth) side and then step up into a col with the ridge rising to your right toward the summit.

If the traverse has you on the south side looking down into Lundin Basin, you have crossed the crest too early. If you top out on a walkable ridge with no notch, you have gone past.

As with the basin approach, the entry from below the notch goes class 3 to a slabby depression, then class 4 to low fifth up the depression, bearing right into the notch.

approach_variants.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
approach_variants.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loose blocky talus on the whole upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block
A snowfield below the summit that can hold firm or icy into midsummer
Eureka Creek ford, cold and high with early-season snowmelt
Faint, unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass, worse on the return
Long, remote, multi-day approach with no cell service
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is marked by water, which is convenient because you should be stopping there anyway. From high camp, traverse northwest to the saddle below Lake Mountain around 7,400 ft, then drop into Lower Monument Basin at roughly 6,100 ft. The outlet creek running from the lake in that basin is the last dependable water on the peak and it sits directly beneath the route; late in the season it can shrink to a trickle but the drainage is still obvious. Fill bottles, then look up and to the left for a ramp system that angles left across the face above you. That ramp is the start of the climbing and it is the feature to identify: it is a continuous weakness slanting up and left, not a gully, and it delivers you onto the south ridge crest at about 6,900 ft. Once you are on the crest the ground flattens into a broad talus highway that runs for well over a mile toward the summit, and that flatness is itself the confirmation that you gained the ridge in the right place rather than on a side rib. Two things mislead near the top. A false summit around 8,000 ft takes a short scramble and looks convincing; the true top is a distinctive leaning horn of granite, so if what you are standing on is not leaning you are not finished. And a steep snowfield sits just below the true summit well into midsummer, which can be crossed with an axe or turned on rock to its left, but should not be glissaded on the way down because it stays firm.

approach_variants.name: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
approach_variants.notes: Just under five miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed pass junction, then a couple of miles and roughly two thousand feet through forest and meadow to the gap. The Boulder Creek side reaches the same pass but is far longer now that the road below it is walked or ridden.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully where several holds are vegetation
A narrow goat ramp on the final approach to the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and basin slopes
Snow near the pass and in the basin below the summit into July
Braided, unmarked climbers' path that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding: Appleton Pass is a true gap with scattered tent pads just below it and maintained trail running on north toward Boulder Lake and east toward Oyster Lake. Leave the tread at the gap and take the climbers' path north along the ridge crest. The base of the real scrambling is a rock step at about 5,800 ft, and the way you know it is a distinct rock horn standing on its south, or left, side — that horn is the marker, and there is nothing else like it on the crest. Below the step you have been on easy heather with a talus basin crossed on the north flank near 5,400 ft; above it you are on exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully and ledge system. Minor outcrops lower on the crest can be turned on either side and are not the step, so do not stop at the first thing that makes you use hands. The narrow goat ramp people talk about comes after the horn, not before it. If you are still traversing level ground with the basin below and no horn in view, you are too low; the notch below the true summit sits near 6,000 ft between the peak's two rocky humps.

approach_variants.name: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
approach_variants.notes: This peak has two genuinely different journeys to it: the western one from the Sol Duc over the High Divide and along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, and the eastern one up the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Both take days. Almost every ascent is a side-summit off a traverse rather than a trip in its own right.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Days of off-trail travel with no quick bail-out and no cell coverage
Dense slide-alder bushwhacking between the Elwha and Elwha Basin
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks
Firm snow on the small glacier below Bear Pass — axe and traction
Long stretches with no maintained trail and no dependable water
approach_variants.baseFinding: Bear Pass is a broad saddle marking the southeastern end of the Bailey Range proper, and from it the ground drops into a flat meadow before the mountain itself. Cross the meadow and contour southeast over scree and lingering snow patches until you are southwest of the summit. That position is the base, and you will know it from the change underfoot: the sidehill traversing stops and the slope above turns into a straight fall-line of moderate, evenly sized scree with a boot track curling left, to the north, onto it. Aside from one brief patch of brush the terrain here is open and the top is in view, so the navigation problem is behind you once you are on that track. Decoys: the ridge running east off Bear Pass is not the summit ridge, and the first obvious scree fan you meet while still traversing leads onto broken ground short of the peak. If the boot track has stopped curling north and you are dropping toward the Queets side, you have gone past the turn.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
approach_variants.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Berge's north and west faces are cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go
A steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
An exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
A short fourth-class step to the true north summit, harder than the rest of the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a broad saddle on the south side at about 7,650 ft, and the way you get to it is a snow finger rather than a slope. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a snow finger and its moat, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

The saddle is where the route leaves the basin. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

The negative marker is the most important thing on this peak and it is about aspect: Berge's north and west faces are cliffy. Parties must stay on the south-west side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

The route-finding rule lower down is a descending traverse, which feels wrong and is right: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

The last obstacle has an elevation and a character: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with slanted slabs and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

The summit is not one point. The true, north summit needs a short fourth-class step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy — the direct line from High Pass does not go, and this approach puts you underneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on both the Buck Creek and Napeequa approaches
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
An exposed 7,840 ft notch linking the two sides of the ridge
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, affecting the drive to Trinity
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The High Pass approach delivers you to the wrong side of the mountain on purpose, and the rule is that you must keep going around. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. The climb is on the south-west side. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

The arrival is the same place for every approach to this peak: the broad saddle on Berge's south side at about 7,650 ft, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

The approach-specific marker on the High Pass line is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

The 7,840 ft notch is the link between the two sides and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

And the same summit warning applies: the true summit is the north one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

approach_variants.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
approach_variants.notes: Read the name on this route with care — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies west of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin, and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail beyond the basin
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August, over a buried climbers' path
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and along the ridge connecting the three summits
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Obstruction Point Road closes for most of the year and is not a route you can count on before July
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is Cameron Pass and the test is the direction you turn out of it: the ridge you climb rises to the east. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. Second test, and it is the one that matters most here: the ridge is a sequence of false summits. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going: the true top is still easy Class 1-2 ground, and steps of Class 3-4 mean you have passed it and are on the traverse. Third test, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. Honest limit and a live disagreement: this route's own summit waypoint calls the east Peak the true 7,190 ft high point, while traverse accounts reach the true summit first from Cameron Pass and then go on to Middle and East. Those cannot both be right. Carry a map, count your summits, and do not treat either the route title or the waypoint name as settled.

approach_variants.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail
approach_variants.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant, reached after a longer approach
Bear canister required; no reliable water above the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical once you are at Cameron Pass: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground all the way to the top. The pass is west of the summit whatever the route title says. The extra test this side needs is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. What going too far looks like: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin
approach_variants.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Many extra miles including a long closed-road walk at each end
A multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical at the pass: the ridge rises east out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground to the true top. The test this side needs is about which valley you are in, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first. Honest limit: this approach is not the one the trailhead record names.

approach_variants.name: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
approach_variants.notes: Carru sits between Osceola and the higher Mount Lago and is almost always climbed as one summit of several on a multi-day trip out of the Harts Pass road end. Two lines reach the country below it: the shorter drops from Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge into the Middle Fork Pasayten, then goes by Fred's Lake and over the ridge crest into upper Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin; the Monument Creek trail is longer with more up and down. Tread through this wilderness is lightly maintained, with blowdown on the valley trail and stretches where the path is fainter on the ground than it looks on a map. The climb itself is short, well under two hours from the base, and unremarkable, essentially a heap of scree and talus with parallel ribs running up it.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Avalanche debris choking the lower gully
Loose scree and talus on the ascent and worse on the descent
Short rock steps and cliff bands within the gully
Steep cliffed north face immediately off the summit crest
Difficult creek crossings during snowmelt
Limited water on the high traverses between the peaks
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a gully, and it identifies itself by being a mess. A scree-and-talus gully drops south off the Carru-Lago col and runs down to meet the trail; where it meets the trail it is typically choked with avalanche debris, meaning snapped timber, jammed branches and rubble piled in the bed. That debris is both the marker and the reason not to start there. Instead, climb the open forest on the right-hand, western side of the gully and step into the bed higher up, at about 6,600 ft, above the worst of the wreckage. Once in the gully the route is contained and hard to lose: scramble up it, weaving round a couple of short rock steps and small cliff bands, until the walls fall back and the ground opens out near the col. That opening-out is the second checkpoint. At that point turn left, to the west, onto the broad southeast ridge and follow the parallel scree ribs to the summit; the ribs run in the direction of travel and any of them will do. The single thing to watch on the upper mountain is which side of the crest you are on. Carru's north side is a steep, cliffed face and is not part of any route here, so if the ground in front of you falls away as a wall rather than a slope you have crossed the crest and should step back south.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
approach_variants.notes: Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 15.3-16.7 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
hazards: A loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col that has changed between seasons — treat published descriptions of it as provisional
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier with a moat at its top whose width varies year to year and by time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk, and refreezing snow in it on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
A thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Extreme remoteness — an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or a helicopter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you south — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

The confirming test is a number and a duration: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

Second test, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you drop down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the Christie Glacier. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a moat forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

What waits at the col, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend
approach_variants.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the November 2017 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
hazards: Road closure at Olympic Hot Springs Road adds 6.2 miles each way and may change season to season
Everything above Low Divide is the same as the Quinault variant: the Class 4 step above the col, the Christie Glacier moat, and the entry couloir
A long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical to the Quinault variant once you are at Low Divide, and that shared test is a good one: from lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft; then down loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

The extra test this side needs is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route leaves maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
approach_variants.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do not follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse below the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice — reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Significant glacier recession, so old descriptions understate the rock and moat work
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival test is a lake you walk across. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to frozen Pea Soup Lake. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice above the low rocks on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

What to do when the lake has melted out, which is the common case from mid-July: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge separating the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the first minor notch at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' left via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

Getting onto the ice, in either season: early, take the snow finger on climbers' right. Late, bypass on climbers' left by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

And the top tells you which summit is which: the glacier leads to the gap between the two highest summits. From the notch, the west summit — on your right — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A scope note that matters to peak-list parties: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

approach_variants.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
approach_variants.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
approach_variants.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
The moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose rotten rock on the class 3 bypass
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the outlet of Pea Soup Lake, and the shoulder above the Foss River is the waypoint that gets you there. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is west until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

From the outlet the finding is the same as from Peggy's Pond: get onto the ice above the low rocks at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' right; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' left and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

The negative test: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.

approach_variants.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
approach_variants.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer
Rockfall in the gully system onto anyone below
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed Skokomish corridor
A very long, remote walk-out from anywhere on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

approach_variants.name: Shellrock Basin and the Lago-Carru col
approach_variants.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached over Robinson Pass and up the Middle Fork Pasayten from either the low Robinson Creek trailhead or the high road end at Slate Peak, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain
Rockfall onto a party stacked below on the face
An enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Difficult crossing of upper Eureka Creek during snowmelt
No shelter from thunderstorms on the open talus and crest
Grizzly and black bear country - proper food storage required
approach_variants.baseFinding: Everything about this climb is on the south side, and the base can be picked up from either of two places. Coming across from the Carru col at about 7,600 ft, the start is where the col's flattish talus stops being flat and tips up into the peak's southwest face, a mixed slope of scree, talus and occasional patches of solid rock with no path, no cairns and no single obvious line, which is itself the signature of this face. Coming up from Shellrock Basin, the start is the toe of the broad south slope above the last stunted trees, at the point where heather gives out and continuous rock begins. In both cases the confirming feature is what is not there: this side carries no cliff band across it. If you are looking up at a wall rather than a long, tedious, uniform slope, you have drifted round onto the wrong aspect and should traverse back south. The mountain's real hazard sits on the far side of the crest, so the top is where care is needed rather than the base. The north side of the summit ridge is an enormous cliff, and the moment you can see straight down you have gone too far north. Which of the crest's several rises is the true high point is not obvious from the face below, so gain the ridge first and judge from up there; a faint boot-worn line runs along the crest and following it is more reliable than picking a top from the slope.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side and the Lake Ouzel high camp
approach_variants.notes: The approach starts north of the border and crosses on foot, so carry a passport. From Chilliwack River Road, turn onto the narrow dirt Depot Creek spur and follow it to a rough turnout where the driving ends; high clearance helps on the upper part. The unmaintained trail climbs the valley, crossing the international boundary at an obelisk and register about two hundred yards in on foot, and a park backcountry permit is required to camp beyond. Near the head of the valley the path crosses the base of a very large waterfall on wet, misty, exposed slabs, including a slippery step that fixed handlines have been rigged for; that crossing is consequential when the rock is wet. Above it a boot track hugs the north edge of the valley and climbs to Lake Ouzel, a flat, sandy, treeless bench that is the shared high camp for this whole group of peaks. From camp, sidehill east and northeast across the bench above the Silver Lake basin toward the peak's south side, using snow coverage where it helps.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September. Earlier there is more snow underfoot, which buries the exposed arete but also hides crevasses on the glaciers used by parties linking this peak with its neighbours. Later the ice turns harder and crevasses open but become easier to see.
hazards: loose, chossy rock in the summit gullies
an exposed knife-edge snow arete partway up the correct gully
crevasse fall on the glaciers used when this peak is combined with its neighbours
the wet, slippery rock step near the falls on the approach
a long, committing cross-border approach with no cell coverage and a multi-day carry-out
approach_variants.baseFinding: Three gullies drop off this summit, and the first one you meet is the wrong one. Coming across the bench toward the south side of the peak, a short band of loose rock guards the final slopes and three gullies come down through it from the summit. The one you reach first as you traverse is the hardest and steepest of the three; do not take it. Keep traversing and take one of the leftmost gullies instead, which go at loose third and fourth class and are easier still when a snow finger is filling them. Two things confirm you are in the right one. Partway up, the correct line crosses an exposed knife-edge snow arete — a genuine, memorable feature, not a snow patch — and above that the ground gives way to a well-defined climbers' path that runs to the top. So: if you are grinding up steep loose fourth class with no arete underfoot and no boot track visible above, back off and move left. If you top out of a gully and find no trodden path, you are on the wrong side of the summit block. The summit itself is rubbly and unassuming and sits a very short distance south of the border. On the way down, reverse the same gully and the same arete rather than improvising a line.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Depot Creek Road trailhead (via Chilliwack, BC)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Chilliwack, BC via Chilliwack River Road ~31.7 miles, then the rough Depot Creek Road spur (high-clearance; passport required to cross the border on foot); unmaintained Depot Creek trail up-valley

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park
approach_variants.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently on April 22, 2025, so this start cannot be reached by car
hazards: Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Committing position with a descent by a different route — plan the carry-over
approach_variants.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you descend, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
approach_variants.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers
Long committing traverse with no quick exit
Same bergschrund and upper mixed-ground hazards as the Mowich approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

approach_variants.name: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
approach_variants.notes: Reached up the North Fork Quinault or by the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge primitive route past Three Lakes and Kimta Peak, or from the Elwha side. Two other lines come in through Noyes Basin and directly up Seattle Creek Basin. Whichever you pick, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Loose scree and talus on both flanks with rockfall onto parties below
Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage steepens
Unbridged fords on the Elwha and North Fork Quinault approaches
A northeast aspect dropping thousands of feet — stay off that side
Extreme remoteness with emergency contact frequently impossible
approach_variants.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.

approach_variants.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
approach_variants.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
An unmarked turnoff and unmapped off-trail travel above the amphitheater
A wide river ford, worse in the afternoon than at dawn
Fallen timber through the burned sections of the lower valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: The turnoff is unmarked — no sign, cairns at best — and getting it right is the whole navigation problem on this route. Above Duckabush Camp, watch for a small feeder creek coming in from climber's-left and follow it up out of the valley. It leads into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of the summit, and that amphitheater is the base: once you are standing in it the climbing is easy Class 2 heather and talus straight up to the summit ridge, so the hard part is behind you. The maintained trail runs on past the turnoff toward the pass, so if you find yourself gaining the pass or arriving at Marmot Lake you have walked past the creek and should drop back down the trail. Snow fills the amphitheater and the slopes above into summer and cornices build on the summit ridge into late June, so carry an axe and treat the crest as possibly unsupported. Water is dependable at the creek and scarce once you leave it — fill up before you start climbing.

approach_variants.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin
approach_variants.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall on the closed valley corridor
Open ground above the basin that is easy to lose in fog
Loose talus on the connecting slopes either side of the col
approach_variants.baseFinding: From First Divide, follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake. That lake is the marker for this whole variant — it is the only standing water in the basin and it sits directly below the two summit humps of Steel, so if you are in an open basin with no lake in it you are in the wrong one. From the lake, drop southwest to the saddle between those humps; the saddle is the base of the climb, and from it you turn north along the summit ridge for the final easy Class 2 stretch to the high point. The direction of that turn is the thing to get right. Duckabush lies beyond the same col to the southwest and reads as the higher, more striking mountain from below, so a party that turns the wrong way off the saddle ends up committed to a different peak. The early-summer cornice and unconsolidated-snow caution applies just as strongly on this side: the crest holds snow late and it is not always attached to the rock beneath it, so stay back from the eastern lip.

approach_variants.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully, with parties above you in it
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
The Great Gendarme's offwidth high on the route, with retreat from there awkward
Cold wind on an exposed crest; parties routinely carry bivy kit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The notch is a place you can sit down, and that is the test. There are two good bivy sites in it. If you have arrived somewhere on the crest with no flat ground, you are not at the notch — you have gained the ridge somewhere else along its length.

The approach to it is a fourth-class gully off the Stuart Glacier, not a scramble up the ridge flank. If the ground you are climbing is open face rather than a defined gully, you are not in the right line.

Orientation at the notch, which settles it: standing in the notch, the whole lower ridge falls away below you to the north and the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far side of it. Everything above you is the upper ridge, and the Great Gendarme is roughly eight or nine pitches up from here. If the big tower is already below you, you have joined the crest above the notch and above two of the route's three named features.

What you have deliberately given up: about 1,200 ft of climbing, including the sustained lieback crack that is the hardest pitch on the complete ridge. So the notch is not a shortcut to be found by accident — a party that meant to climb the complete ridge and ends up here has walked past its own route. Confirm which climb you are on before you start up.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 rock in the gully with parties above
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse; buried creek channels
Couloir can be entirely melted out late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.

approach_variants.name: Torment Basin climbers' path
approach_variants.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
approach_variants.season: midsummer once brush is passable
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach — fewer parties, less current beta on conditions
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.

approach_variants.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
approach_variants.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October
hazards: Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
A wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Loose pea gravel over hardpack on the lowest switchback set
A steep open slope below the summit ridge that holds consolidated snow
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is no scramble on this route, so the questions that matter are which fork and which top. Above Camp Windy, at about 5,500 ft and roughly three miles in, the trail meets the Silver Lakes Trail: stay right and uphill. The left fork drops toward Silver Lakes on loose, unmaintained ground and is not the route. You have taken the right branch when the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the grade eases markedly for the final stretch, with the last quarter mile crossing open, low-angle grassy and rocky tundra rather than anything steep. The high ground is a broad, flat ridge with more than one apparent top. The south summit is the true high point; the popular viewpoint where most people stop and turn round sits a short, easy walk below the actual crown, and the north summit further along the crest is lower still. Rock outcrops on the south top give the only wind shelter up there. Early season, snow on the upper meadow and on the steep open slope gaining the ridge is where the tread is easiest to lose in flat light.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat over Saska Pass and Snow Brushy Creek
approach_variants.notes: A long, largely off-trail approach through burned country for a summit that is barely a scramble. From the North Fork Entiat road end the tread runs up-valley past the Fern Lake spur to the Pyramid Mountain junction, which is the usual last camp with water; fill there, because the drainages between it and the pass are seasonal and often dry. Gain Saska Pass by climbing the drainage directly rather than following the sidehill traverse, which is slower and more tiring across scree. From the pass you lose about 1,500 ft into the Snow Brushy burn, where the tread is gone entirely and ash-covered slopes and fallen snags erase any line, then regain nineteen hundred feet or so out of the creek — that descent and reclimb are what make the day long, not the peak. A separate approach exists up the Entiat River trail and the sheep driveway from the south, also through heavy fire blowdown.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe early
hazards: Loose scree on the headwall below the pass, and worse for anyone climbing beneath you
Burn-zone deadfall and standing snags with no surviving tread, so a cairn line cannot be relied on
Scarce water above the last creek crossings
A steep, loose couloir on the final approach to the crest saddle
Long remote off-trail travel with little or no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is the saddle on the Chelan Mountains crest immediately south of the peak, reached by a steep couloir of loose rock, and the thing to know before you get there is that the true summit is hidden from it. Standing on the saddle you see a rocky bump close by to the south — a point just over 7,760 ft — and a broad, easy-angled slope running north. The bump is not the mountain and is only a short side trip for the view; the slope is your line. Turn north and climb the south-facing talus, keeping to the west side of the crest where the scrambling stays easiest, and the top only reveals itself in the last few hundred feet. The rock underfoot changes noticeably as you go: poor scree low down where the burn ends, then firmer blocks on the crest that make a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk. If the ground ahead drops away toward the Emerald Peak basin instead of rising, you have crossed the crest too far east.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead at the end of FR 5606

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A long, exposed and dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side, periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long walk back over the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Pace it off from the left-flank classic: this route starts about 100 feet to the right of it, on the west side of the south face. That is a measurable distance rather than a description, and it is what makes the start findable — everything else on this end of the face is identified relative to the same outside corner.

So the procedure in poor visibility is two steps. First find the outside corner where the south face turns onto the west side. The classic left-flank line starts just right of that corner. Then walk right roughly a hundred feet along the base. That is where you are.

What tells you you have overshot: keep walking right along the base and the ground under the middle of the face is where the summit route starts, and beyond that the two large V-features of the next line along. Reaching either means you have gone several hundred feet too far.

What tells you you are short: a large roof at the base means you have crossed the corner onto the west face entirely and are two routes left.

First-pitch confirmation: a short crack and slab leading to a corner. It is not a long lead and it is not hard. The long, exposed, somewhat dirty face crack is the second pitch. If your first pitch is long and dirty you have started one pitch too high or on the wrong line.

And the top-out check: this route finishes on the West Ridge, not the summit — the same as its two neighbours on this flank. That shared finish is why they share one rappel descent on the north side.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, round the corner onto the west face
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This one faces west rather than south, so it comes into the sun later in the day and is a cold morning start
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
A short aid section through steep terrain at mid-height
Shared natural rappel anchors on the north side that have been rebuilt and relocated over the years
A west aspect: late sun, cold mornings, and afternoon weather arriving unseen from behind the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The roof at ground level is the marker, and it is the only one you need. This route starts underneath a large roof formation at the very base — climbing it is the first pitch, straight off the deck. No other line at this end of the peak starts under a roof. Standing under a big overhang means you are here.

Which side of the corner you are on decides it. The south face turns an outside corner onto the west side. This route is left of that corner, i.e. on the west face; the left-flank south-face classic is just right of it. So: corner on your right, roof over your head, west face — correct. Corner on your left and no roof — you have stepped back onto the south face and are on a different climb.

Aspect as a sanity check: this one faces west. If you have been standing in the sun all morning, you are on the south face and not here.

Mid-route confirmation: there is a pair of rock features partway up that the route is named for, with a steep fingery crack running between them. If you never pass between two distinct features, you are not on this line.

And the top: this route joins its neighbour's final corner crack, so the last pitch is shared and the summit is not reached directly — you finish on the West Ridge. That shared finish is also why the rappel descent is the same one.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
