approach_variants.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow, and a fatal history
A 5.11+ crux on the first pitch, so retreat decisions come early
A loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side — one bolted station near the top, gear and slung naturals below
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Core Zone camping needs a permit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Fifty feet left of the standard South Face route. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

The first pitch is the check, and it is a brutal one. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

What the first pitch looks like from the ground, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing left-slanting crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

Belay confirmation: pitch one ends at a two-bolt anchor after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

And the named pitch higher up: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

Descent note that affects the approach decision: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
approach_variants.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,600 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, right and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Cross-country navigation over slabs with no tread for the last mile
Core Zone camping requires a permit that most parties do not have
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Go to the outside corner and start just right of it. The left flank of the south face ends in an outside corner — the arête where the south face turns the corner onto the west side — and this route begins just to the right of it, on a right-leaning crack system leading to a stembox.

That corner is the anchor for the whole left end of the face, and the three routes here are placed off it:
  - Left of the corner, on the west face proper: a line with a large roof at its base, sometimes called the Elephant Ear.
  - Just right of the corner: this route.
  - About 100 ft further right: another four-pitch line to the West Ridge.
So if you are under a roof, you have gone one route too far left; if you have walked a hundred feet right of the corner, one too far right.

The honest warning about where this route ends, because it is the best single check that you are on the left flank at all: this line and its immediate neighbours top out on the west ridge, not on the summit. Only the classic line at the middle of the face reaches the true summit. If you have come for the summit and started here, you have an extra scramble at the top and you started on the wrong route.

Sequence check: right-leaning cracks to a stembox, then a roof and hand-crack pitch, then slabby and wide ground past a chimney with loose rock, then a final splitter corner. Five pitches, about 450 ft. A seven-pitch line with two big V-features low down is Beckey-Davis, well to your right.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain to climber's right, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Rappel descent on the north side is shared by several south-face routes and backs up when busy
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse northeast to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of deep chimneys on the face. The route starts to the left of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep white granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just below some shrubby pines. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

approach_variants.name: Shellrock Pass camp and the south side
approach_variants.notes: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Sheer, seldom-seen north face immediately off the summit
Loose talus and a steep waterfall drainage on off-route descent lines
Short exposed scrambling on the connecting ridge to the south
Brush-choked valley approaches and heavy blowdown
Faint or obscured tread near the Eureka Creek turn
Extreme remoteness with no fast rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are two ways onto this peak and each has its own recognisable base. From the south, the base is the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle at about 7,800 ft, a genuine meadow holding a small tarn, unmistakable ground after miles of talus and the last water on the day. From that saddle the south slopes rise as open alpine tundra, scree and easy talus and there is nothing to find; you simply walk up. Getting to the saddle from the Shellrock Pass camp means gaining the crest north of camp and travelling over or around the shoulder of Mount Lago, with a short exposed step or two on the connecting ridge near the two rock points south of Dot. From the north and west the base is a saddle at about 7,250 ft overlooking Ptarmigan Lake, and the marker there is better still: a well-trodden boot path leaves the maintained trail at the Tatoosh Buttes junction around 6,950 ft and heads due south across the hillside and over a low rise on Tamarack Ridge, and following it to the saddle puts you at the foot of the north ridge, which is broad and easy. Whichever side you come from, the same rule identifies the route: the ground under you should stay rounded, open and tundra-covered. Ptarmigan's north face is sheer and seldom seen, so any point where the slope stops falling away gently and starts breaking off is the signal that you have wandered onto the wrong aspect and should move back south.

approach_variants.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
approach_variants.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. A longer alternative comes in over War Creek Ridge from the Williams Creek side and can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, but it joins the same finish. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and the summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower trail, which sees little maintenance
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying on the climber's right bank, roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

approach_variants.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
approach_variants.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
hazards: The Le Conte Glacier is actively crevassed — rope up and carry a rescue kit
The Red Ledge is genuinely serious when banked with snow, which is common into early July
Snow in the west basin reaches 35-40 degrees near its top and softens through the day
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Le Conte-Sentinel col is the reference: a flat notch at the top of the glacier carrying dry gravel bivy platforms, the only level dry ground for a long way in any direction. From the notch the peak's west side presents one continuous basin of snow running up to a rock face, and that snow is the route. Its top is the only place on the face where a broad, walkable ledge cuts leftward, to the north, beneath a short cliff band. Those two features together are the proof: continuous snow steepening as it rises, and an obvious ledge running left off the top of it. If the snow you have chosen tops out against blank rock with no ledge leading off it, you are too far south in the basin. If you are on bare rock with no snow beneath you at all, you have wandered onto the east side, which degrades into rotten rock and steep snow — that is the side parties get wrong on the descent, and it is not the route.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: The long way in from the west. Start at the Downey Creek trailhead off the Suiattle River Road and work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor — Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek — on rugged, largely off-trail ground with real bushwhacking and glacier travel. Budget a full day, often two, before you are anywhere near rock. This is an experienced-mountaineers approach and nothing about it is a walk-in.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the bushwhacking is out of snow and the glaciers are travellable.
hazards: Open moat between glacier ice and the foot of the face; it hangs free enough that a rappel to the glacier has come off the rock well above the snow
Loose, poor-quality rock from the first pitch upward
Glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the approach and directly below the climb
Multi-day committing approach with no realistic quick exit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The east face of this peak rises directly out of the glacier, so the base of the climb is the ice-to-rock junction and the moat is the marker. Traverse the glacier under the east side until you find the point where the face rears up clean out of the ice rather than sitting back behind broken ground. The start is a finger-and-hand crack system you can step into straight out of the moat and follow for about a rope length to a ledge — if you cannot enter the crack from the moat without first scrambling talus, you are not at it. Expect the moat to be open and to need gear or a bridge; a recorded rappel back onto this glacier from above hung free over it, so the gap at the bottom is a permanent feature of this side rather than a bad year. Negative markers: if the wall in front of you is catching afternoon sun, you have crossed the crest and are on the west side of the peak; if you are looking up at a pair of clean dihedrals side by side, you are around on the ridge south of the summit at the start of the ridge route.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek from the east
approach_variants.notes: The other documented way into this range comes from the east, via the lake ferry and the long trail up Agnes Creek before leaving it for the brush. Parties using it camp on rock ridges above the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing on the same day. It is not a shortcut — the bushwhack off the trail takes most of a day on its own — but it puts you on the glacier side of the crest, which is the side this route starts from.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach with a full day of brush before any alpine ground
Crevasses and a persistent moat at the foot of the east faces
Loose rock throughout the climb
The peak is one of four closely spaced summits on one crest, easily confused from below
approach_variants.baseFinding: Camping on the ridges above the glacier puts you looking straight across at the east faces, which is the one view that makes this route findable: pick the line before you drop onto the ice, because from the glacier itself the faces foreshorten and the individual crack systems disappear. On the ice, work under the peak until the face rises clean from the moat and a finger-and-hand crack can be entered directly out of it. Negative marker: the peak is the southernmost of the four named summits on this short crest, so if you are still under a summit with more towers to the south of you, you are one peak too far north.

approach_variants.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
approach_variants.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Loose blocky rock on the talus approach and the summit ridge, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and ice in the basin and the summit gully into early August, and bullet-hard patches
An exposed class 4 ledge traverse just below the summit with real fall consequences
In-situ slings at the crux that are aging tat and need backing up before they are weighted
Extreme remoteness — assume a multi-day evacuation or a helicopter for any serious injury
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The most important thing to know about this approach is that below 7,400 ft it is indistinguishable from Goode Mountain's. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

The counting test is the notch, and the word is right-most. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the right-most one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

Cross to the north side of that notch and the ground changes character completely: a fun ledge traverse on the backside of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. If you have not crossed to the north side, you have not found the ledge traverse, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

Confirm on the ledge: it includes a squeeze under a slight overhang, and there are in-situ slings at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

The last move is a choice, not a crux: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its left side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

And know which top you want: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the easternmost is the true high point.

approach_variants.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A full traverse of both Fury summits simply to reach the saddle
Glaciated terrain between Luna Col and the Fury summits
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no independent descent
Very little published route detail, and the peak itself is imprecisely located
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is a saddle between two named summits and you reach it by having crossed both summits of Fury. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there. Arrival: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the northwest ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. Why there is so little here, said plainly: Swiss Peak has one described route and no first-ascent record, the peak itself is not precisely located, and nothing published locates a feature at the foot of the southwest face. What is locatable is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col. What going too far looks like: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.

approach_variants.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length and is described only in outline, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A long off-trail ridge sequence with no maintained tread
No independent descent; exiting the range means committing to one of the long approach drainages
Very little published detail for either approach to this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Pickell Pass the south side of Swiss is climbed directly, and the test is that you are going up rather than along. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

How to know you are at Pickell Pass rather than another saddle on the same ridge system: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's northeast ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

Why this side may be the better choice, as a planning fact rather than a landmark: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.

approach_variants.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
approach_variants.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
hazards: Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter — be off it by early afternoon
Loose rock and talus on the ridge crest
A long, essentially waterless final push above the lake
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Iced blocks in shoulder season, which turn an easy scramble into something considerably more serious
Mosquitoes in the lake basins through mid-July
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the lake the trail keeps climbing for roughly another mile, crossing a saddle at about 7,900 ft on the peak's southeast side, and then runs into the broad southeast ridge of the mountain. The point where the tread meets that crest is the base — everything to there is walking on a path, and everything above it is off it. The ridge itself is easy and broad, so the confirmation is the last few hundred feet rather than the first: the crest steepens into a field of large, mostly stable blocks that wants hands only occasionally, with a few more exposed steps possible right at the top. The neighbour to watch for is the similar summit under a mile north along the same crest, which is a comparable height, a comparable walk and shares a lake name with this one in places — parties do link the two, but if you have walked north along easy open ridge for the better part of a mile you are on the other peak.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. Leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is Whistler Mountain above Rainy Pass in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Climb until the forest opens. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A meadow basin below the west ridge and gully complex, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

From the basin, trend south and southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col and basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat. That col is the aiming point, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the broad west ridge, or the shallow gully just north of it, to the summit shoulder.

The last section is the one that confirms you are on the summit line rather than a neighbouring gully: a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall, over downsloping slabs and loose gravel. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The trailhead is unmarked and the path start is a tree-line edge, so the find is at the road rather than on the mountain. The pullout is 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake Trailhead coming from Rainy Pass. If you have reached the Blue Lake Trailhead, you have driven 0.7 mile too far. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a stand of trees begins, and the boot path leaves from its west edge.

Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. A level section of ridge is the arrival, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit. The alternative, which is also correct: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

So the decision at 6,800 ft is a real fork and both branches work: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

The negative test against the other approach, which matters because both start within three miles of each other on the same highway: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a meadow basin at 6,100 ft below the west ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the south ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

approach_variants.name: Trail 342 from Long Swamp
approach_variants.notes: This is the easternmost of the high peaks here and by far the least technical, being a trail walk with a very short scramble stapled on the end, so the real work is the drive. Long gravel forest roads out of Loomis reach Long Swamp Campground, where Trail 342 starts and climbs steadily through burned lodgepole and recovering meadow to a camp with water partway up and then out onto open, treeless ridge. A shorter trail comes in from the Cathedral Driveway trailhead a few miles further west but is overgrown in stretches from lack of use, and a third start at Iron Gate involves the roughest driving of the three. Water on the upper trail is limited and seasonal, so carry enough for a long day.
approach_variants.season: Late June to early October
hazards: Long trail mileage with limited seasonal water on the upper half
Fully exposed, treeless summit ridge in wind and lightning
Faint, braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch
Standing fire-killed snags along the burned lower trail in wind
Long gravel road driving far from any town
approach_variants.baseFinding: The trail does not go to the top, which is the single most useful thing to know here. Tread climbs to a junction and high point below and south of the summit at roughly 8,100 ft and then begins contouring and descending onward toward Horseshoe Basin and the Boundary Trail. The base of the scramble is exactly where the trail stops climbing. Standing on the plateau at that point, the summit rocks are obvious: they stand up as a small blocky pyramid of about three hundred feet, and there is nothing else nearby that looks like it. Leave the constructed tread and take the cairned, braided path up open talus on the south side of that pyramid; it is easy blocky scrambling and takes only a few minutes. The confirmations at the top are physical and worth checking, because the plateau carries other rises. Benchmark nails are set in the summit rock at the site of the old lookout, and remnants of the lookout's telephone line still run down the northwest slope toward the saddle, so if you can find the wire you are on the right high point. The way to know you have overshot is comfort: if you are walking downhill on good graded tread with the summit rocks behind your shoulder, you have passed the turn and should come back to the trail's high point.

approach_variants.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and the Carbon Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Everyone walks in from White River Campground, and the walking is over quickly. The Glacier Basin Trail is maintained for about three and a half miles to the basin at roughly 5,900 ft, which holds the last running water you will see until the descent brings you down to Camp Schurman. Above the basin there is no trail: a boot track climbs snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, and from the far side of the pass you drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and stay roped for the rest of the trip. The counter-clockwise traverse under Mount Ruth and around the toe of Curtis Ridge is the part that decides the day, because it runs directly beneath Willis Wall and both walls shed rock and ice more freely once the sun is on them. Most parties split the approach with a bivy on lower Curtis Ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,600 ft, right beside the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier, and it is the only place on the whole approach where you get a head-on look at the route to pick your line. Curtis Ridge is broad and deceptive in cloud and parties repeatedly think they have arrived when they have not; the rule everyone repeats is to stay low and, when in doubt, angle down and right. If what you are looking over is not a mellow fifty-foot talus slope, you are too high, and climbing further only cliffs you out. A climbing permit is required and this line carries its own briefing, so sort both before driving up rather than on the morning you want to leave.
approach_variants.season: Early May to mid-June
hazards: Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall onto the Carbon Glacier traverse, worsening through the day
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier onto the west side of the Carbon basin
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings
The moat between glacier and rock at the foot of the ridge, which turns parties around outright
Rockfall into Thumb Rock camp, which has been swept out by slides off the tower opposite
Sustained steep ice to around 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming off Curtis Ridge everything underfoot is glacier, so the ridge has to be picked out by shape and by what stands either side of it. Where Liberty Ridge meets the Carbon it is a rock nose, a prow of broken volcanic rock at roughly 8,450 to 8,600 ft rather than a snow slope, and often the place you can watch rocks peeling off. Memorise the compass check, because it holds everywhere on the climb. Facing uphill, Willis Wall is on your left, to the east, and the Liberty Wall is on your right, to the west. If the big wall is on your right hand as you look up, you are on the wrong feature. Cross the Carbon up climber's right of the main icefall and aim for the nose. The real crux of the approach is the moat where the glacier pulls away from the rock, and parties are stopped here more often than anywhere else on the climb — not because the ridge is hard to see, but because there is no way across the gap that day. You can gain the crest from either flank or straight up the toe, at roughly 8,600 to 8,800 ft. The east flank is steeper and carries more rock bands, so most parties cross onto the west flank as soon as they are on the crest and stay there up to camp. Which side actually goes is decided by the moat and the crevasses rather than by preference, so scout instead of committing to the first weakness. In poor visibility the confirmation is not at the toe at all, it is above it: Thumb Rock, a 300 ft gendarme of broken volcanic rock at somewhere around 10,500 ft, with a second loose tower opposite it and barely room for two small tents in the saddle between. Parties fogged out at the base have started to retreat and turned around again only when Thumb Rock showed through a break in the cloud, so if you are unsure, wait for a window and look up rather than along. You have gone too far west if the ground opens into the Carbon basin beneath the Liberty Wall's hanging ice; crevasses routinely push parties that way, and the next spine past that wall is Ptarmigan Ridge, a different climb off a different camp.

approach_variants.name: Longmire, the Wonderland Trail and Indian Henry's Hunting Ground
approach_variants.notes:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail heading southwest. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.
approach_variants.season: May through September; the lower cleaver is best while it still holds snow, since it becomes loose scree once bare
hazards: Kautz Creek crossing washed out by glacial debris flows
Rockfall from parties above on the loose lower cleaver
Sustained loose choss and scree with no established line
Knife-edge crest section, exposed once melted out
Very long approach with no bail-out — a retreat is the full walk back to Longmire
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the col north of Pyramid Peak, at about 6,400 ft, and getting into that col is where people go wrong.

From Point 6631 you drop north-northeast a short way to a saddle. It is a scree and loose-boulder col, and it is ugly — that is the correct place. There is an easier descent line into it than the obvious one, and trip reports record missing it and taking the worst ground; look for the line before you commit, and note it for the way back.

From the col the cleaver rises continuously in front of you and does not stop. There is no single track and no cairned line: the lower cleaver is loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, and the route-finding is yours.

The test that you are on the cleaver and not off it is what is on either side. You should be on a broad rubbly crest with the South Tahoma Glacier falling away to your north (climber's left) and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to your south (climber's right). If a glacier is underfoot you have left the cleaver — this route is defined by not being on one.

An easy, clean start is the wrong sign. If the ground out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you are probably contouring around the peak rather than gaining the cleaver. Travel only improves higher, above about 7,000 ft, where the rock firms up and, early in the season, continuous snow and goat tracks take over.

Higher still the crest includes a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow melts off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies onto the Kautz Cleaver at roughly 12,200–12,600 ft.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,880-3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall throughout the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge
Cliff bands below the south-west face that have caught descending parties in icy or snow-covered conditions
A narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest that has to be avoided rather than followed
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July in heavy years
Heavy blowdown and washed-out sections on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past wildfires and storm damage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the col and the direction off it is west. From the basin camp, about 600 ft of gain on talus, scree or lingering snow reaches the Emerald-Saska Col at roughly 7,700 ft — a notch on the south ridge with a peak on either side. From the col, head west toward Saska. Emerald is the other way. If you leave the col climbing east you are on the neighbouring peak's ground.

The positive test is that you do not stay on the crest. The connecting ridge is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line drops slightly onto its west flank to pick up an obvious scree-and-rock gully, then follows a cairned rising traverse back toward the crest. West flank, gully, cairned rising traverse. A party grimly balancing along the crest itself has missed the line rather than found the hard way.

The finish is counted in feet, not features: roughly 300 ft of final Class 3 on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold — nothing here is fixed and no rope is standard, although the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them.

The descent marker is a warning with a documented consequence: cliff bands sit below the south-west face. Stay well clear of them when the ground is snow-covered or icy. A winter party misjudging that descent line in icy conditions lost a ski over those cliffs. In early-to-mid season the continuous snow below the col gives a glissade or boot-ski; by August and September the same ground is loose scree and dirt that has to be walked slowly.

Loose rock is the theme of the whole cirque. Helmet, and do not stack the party directly above one another, from the moment you leave the basin.

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
approach_variants.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up beside the southeast ridge. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is outside the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto Bean Creek Trail near the start
Ingalls Creek ford is a genuine obstacle in early season or after rain
Loose talus in the basin; hard snow in shoulder season warranting axe and crampons
Long, remote approach — a partial day just to reach the base, so plan a car-camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trail closures following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — verify before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climb follows the crest of the southeast ridge, which rises from the Ingalls Creek side to the southeast spire, the lowest of Argonaut's three summits. The lower pitches are blocky, lichen-covered and awkward, which is the sign you are on the ridge proper.

Low down, the ridge can be crossed at a notch near 6,750 ft between the south slope and Porcupine Basin; that crossing is a way between the two drainages, not a feature of the climb.

Above the southeast spire, two single-rope rappels or one double-rope rappel take you into the notch, and the route continues to the true summit on the west spire.

approach_variants.name: Chickamin Glacier to the snow finger between the main and south spires
approach_variants.notes: From the Chikamin-Dome col, a descending traverse of roughly ninety minutes drops onto the Chickamin Glacier and reaches a snow dome and rock outcrop at about 7,000 ft, closely below the peak; many parties move camp here or day-climb from the col. From that outcrop, boot up to the snow finger running between the main spire and the south spire. On the snow approach, take the first col south of the south peak — the long-standing published advice to use the second col south of it has been corrected by parties who followed it, and the first is the right one. Descent reverses the line by rappel: from the top of the chimney, traverse to the notch, downclimb to a second station, rappel to the ledge above the glacier, then one more onto the snow.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Crevasse hazard on the Dome and Chickamin Glaciers — rope, and crevasse rescue gear
Loose rock in the basalt dike section
Wild exposure on the narrow summit ridge
A summit horn only one party member can stand on at a time
approach_variants.baseFinding: A reddish-black basalt dike is the line, and it is softer than everything around it. From the 7,000 ft snow dome and rock outcrop, boot up the snow finger between the main and south spires; from a breach in that finger, a short wall leads to a broad ledge, then leftward to a steep dihedral of black rock whose top fifteen feet is the exposed 5.6 crux on solid granite. Above it, traverse left on Class 3 granite into a distinctive dike of reddish-black basalt — this is the feature that carved the gunsight notch in the first place, eroding faster than the granite either side, so if the rock you are on is the same colour as its neighbours you are not in the dike. It scrambles easily, if loosely, to the high notch between the main and north spires. There a vertical headwall blocks a direct exit: descend about twenty feet and traverse right across steep, solid, well-broken rock into a shallow parallel gully. Short chimneys and cracks to 5.5 end at the crest beside a large horn slung with old rappel tat — that horn is not the summit; the summit is a separate horn about the size of a barstool further along the ridge.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer left to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues west, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
The steep steps turning to bare ice or dry-tooling ground later in the season
Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp
An unmarked, often snow-covered off-trail turn out of the Mountaineer Creek valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: The north ridge rock rib decides it, and the side it is on is the answer. From the basin you are looking at four things in a row: the Sherpa Glacier, the Ice Cliff Glacier, the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, and beyond it the Stuart Glacier. You want to be past the rib. So: if the North Ridge rib is on your left (east) you are on the Stuart Glacier and correct. If it is still on your right you have not gone far enough west and are on the Ice Cliff side. That is the same test the Ice Cliff Glacier route uses, read in the opposite direction, and it is the reliable one in cloud because it does not depend on seeing the summit. Second test — what the couloir leads to. This couloir does not go to the summit. It goes to a notch in the west ridge, which is on the far side of the mountain from where you camped. If the line you are looking up appears to head for the top of the peak, you are looking at the wrong feature. Third, the shape. Entry is at about 7,800 ft and the couloir narrows above you before it widens again — moderate snow, then a short steep step, then a second shorter one, then an open snowfield. A line that is uniformly wide with no steps is not this one. And the negative test: no hanging ice cliff or serac band should be above you anywhere. If there is one, you are back on the Ice Cliff Glacier, on the wrong side of the rib.

approach_variants.name: Bird Creek Meadows and Sunrise Camp, on the Yakama Reservation side
approach_variants.notes:
This is the southeast side of the mountain and the approach crosses Yakama Nation land, which makes it an access problem before it is a climbing problem. A tribal-use permit for Tract D is required, bought at the fee station on entry at the Mirror Lake gate — it cannot be obtained in advance — and it is only available when the area is open to non-tribal use. Historically that window has run from about the start of July to the start of October for non-members. The area has also been closed outright in some years, so confirm with the Yakama Nation before building a trip around this approach; there is no alternative way in from this side.

From the Bird Creek Meadows parking area (about 5,576–5,700 ft), the trail is easy to follow to roughly 6,700 ft. Above that it is route-finding: any number of lines through moraine, scree and glacier remnants lead up to Sunrise Camp at about 8,300 ft. Carry a map — locating the camp is the part people get wrong. Trailhead to camp is about 3–4 hours.

Sunrise Camp sits at the base of the Mazama Glacier, tucked between the glacier and a small rock hill, with hand-built rock shelters. It is a fine fair-weather camp and a poor one otherwise: it is exposed to winds that can reach hurricane strength, and to rockfall off the glacier. The rock walls help, but only somewhat.

From camp to summit is about 5 hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer; non-tribal access to this side has historically been limited to a mid-summer to early-autumn window
hazards: Tribal-use permit required and only sold at the gate, in a limited seasonal window — no advance purchase, and the area has been closed in some years
Route-finding through moraine and scree above 6,700 ft to locate Sunrise Camp
Rockfall off the glacier onto Sunrise Camp
Extreme wind exposure at camp
Bergschrunds around 9,500 ft
Mistaking Piker's Peak, where the route tops out, for the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts directly above camp — the first ground you cross after leaving Sunrise Camp is the glacier itself, so the recognition problem here is finding camp, not finding the base.

Sunrise Camp: at roughly 8,300 ft, a flat with rock wind shelters, wedged between the toe of the Mazama Glacier on one side and a small rock hill on the other. If you are on open moraine with no rock hill beside you, you are short of it or off to one side; the terrain between 6,700 and 8,300 ft has many plausible lines and only some of them end at the camp.

Above camp the sequence is legible. Long stretches of glacier at about 40 degrees, then bear right onto the headwall proper, which runs about 45 degrees and is where pickets earn their place. Bergschrunds appear around 9,500 ft. The glacier narrows as it climbs.

The top is where the route makes you choose. Nearing Piker's Peak — the south summit at 11,644 ft — you can exit left onto easy 25–30 degree ground, or stay right for a short technical finish: roughly 40 ft of 60–70 degree snow and ice on the southeast corner, worth two or three screws.

Critical negative marker at the top: Piker's Peak is not the summit of Mount Adams. When the ground flattens out you have reached the south summit; the true summit is a further dome across the plateau to the north, with the geographic high point to the east. This route tops out on the false summit by design, so treat the flattening as a halfway signal rather than an arrival.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge, the Hogsback and the Coleman-Roosevelt crossing
approach_variants.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles. Take the right-hand climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft beside the Coleman Glacier, the same camp used for the Coleman-Deming and the North Ridge.

From camp the route ropes up and heads northeast, crossing the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Expect two to three hours of glacier travel through a crevasse field before low-to-moderate snow ramps lead to the foot of the ridge.
approach_variants.season: spring to early summer
hazards: crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers
bergschrunds below and on the ridge
loose rock on the ridge, worse as the snow melts out
icefall on the ramps that skirt the towers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ridge is reached by traversing northeast from the Hogsback camps across the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Aim for the foot of the ridge at about 7,500-7,800 ft, where low-angle snow ramps lead up onto the crest.

The Cockscomb Tower, about 300 ft high, stands well above the base and is passed on its east side by steep snow; if you are already beside it, you are far above the start. If you have crossed only the Coleman and are still west of the Roosevelt, you have not reached this ridge yet.
